rv.q: Ultimately this is a powerful meditation on morality, fuelled by the assertion that people can – and do – change.
But still this play often feels overly didactic, with little moral complication, and little to surprise or challenge existing views you might have of any of the people involved...
James Graham’s drama about a single-punch killing builds to an emotionally devastating climax
Punch is one of the few narratives that offers a route out of what feels like a constant downward spiral.
Punch does not leave a dry eye in the house, yet Graham laces his script with surprising bouts of humour...Directed by Adam Penford, the production is strikingly unfussy.
It's a highwire act that just about works, largely thanks to a confident writer, an acutely perceptive director and a brilliant central performance from Shields.
Punch demonstrates Graham’s ability to distil a complex and painful history into something theatrically engaging, even if the script occasionally reins itself in.
The emotional power which the play generates, gradually builds and takes ahold of the audience, particularly in its latter stages and was palpable on opening night.
Punch is theatre at its very best and is, once again, a huge hit.
This remarkable story of the power of restorative justice is performing for a limited time only, and we'd urge everyone to see it.

Graham brilliantly shows rather than tells us how group therapy, an overworked but empathetic social worker (a wry Emma Pallant) and the formal exchange of letters with his victim's parents help to save Jacob from spiralling downwards.
There is no denying the emotional wallop delivered by Penford’s production and the performances at its core.

cn.t: James Graham's true-crime drama about a fatal punch earns widespread acclaim for its raw emotional power and nuanced exploration of restorative justice, though some find its state-of-the-nation themes overstretched.
